provenance: Galerie Lelong, New York | Acquired from the above by the present owner | | Exhibited | Huesca, Centro de Arte y Naturaleza, Fundación Beulas, Territorios que Importan, Género, arte y ecología, 18 October 2018 - 20 January 2019 | | | | Ana Mendieta's work endures as a quiet yet unyielding force, tracing the profound bond between human beings and the earth. Untitled presents a simple, intimate gesture in the outline of a female figure inscribed on a delicate leaf. Within this modest form lies the complexity of Mendieta's practice - an oeuvre that has moved through many contexts over time: essentialism, feminism, anti-colonial critique, and the continual transgression of artistic boundaries, perfectly exemplifying the artist's lasting relevance and her remarkable ability to speak across generations. The fragility of the leaf in the present work reflects the vulnerability of the female body, yet its preservation and resilience suggest an enduring strength - a quiet assertion of the body's power to persist. | | Part of a generation of artists whose practices no longer conformed to the conventions of exhibition-making and collecting, Mendieta's work resists containment in any single category. Instead, it exists somewhere between acts and object. In the present piece, she inscribed upon a green leaf, an element that in its very nature was destined to shift, dry, and decay. Time itself becomes a collaborator, transforming the work as matter changes state. Like her performances, Untitled embodies this delicate tension between permanence and impermanence, capturing both a gesture of presence and its inevitable passage into transformation. | | Drawing was an integral part of Mendieta's practice which developed from her years as a student in the Intermedia department at Iowa University. Her sketchbooks from that period are filled with ideas that would later materialise in her earth-body and Silueta works. Throughout her career the artist kept a detailed record of her practice, documenting new, iconic performance pieces and interventions, yet it was only in the early 1980s that drawing emerged as a distinct body of work. Initially, Mendieta experimented with amate, a bark paper made by the Otomí people of Mexico, historically used in ritual contexts since pre-Columbian times. Soon after, she discovered the leaves of the Clusia rosea, also known as the autograph tree, whose thick, leathery surfaces could be inscribed by scratching away the dark outer skin to reveal a lighter layer beneath. Long used by Caribbean schoolchildren for writing and by Spanish colonial soldiers as makeshift playing cards, these leaves carried both everyday and historical resonances. Onto them, Mendieta etched figures that echoed her contemporaneous 'goddess' sculptures, evoking the imagery of Cuba's Taíno culture. In this act, she turned a material once used by colonisers into a site for the preservation and reanimation of indigenous and ancestral forms. Untitled beautifully exemplifies Mendieta's carefully considered process of memorialisation by recording and preserving her memory through an act that honours her native Cuban culture. | | Forging connections with the Earth and the cosmos was central to Mendieta's output, a concern that permeated her whole output but which is perhaps most evident in the Silueta Series. In this emblematic body of work the artist placed her body within the landscape, later also highlighting its absence and the traces she had left within it. Explained by Mendieta herself, "My art is the way I re-establish the bonds that unite me to the universe". Whether inscribed in the earth, or drawn onto it, the body became a conduit for reestablishing ties with the natural world and for articulating a fractured sense of identity. Later in her career, she extended this exploration into freestanding sculptures, in which the personal and performative gave way to archetypal forms, muting ritual presence in favour of lasting, three-dimensional objects. Influenced by artists such as Vito Acconci, Lynda Benglis, Chris Burden, Bruce Nauman, and the Fluxus group, Mendieta continually pushed the boundaries of what art could be. Earth, its elements, and the body itself became at once her medium and her message, expressing the profound, universal bond between humanity and nature, while transcending cultural, social, and historical confines. | | Untitled ultimately invites us to inhabit a space where fragility and strength coexist, where the ephemeral becomes eternal through gesture, trace, and transformation. Mendieta's work does not merely represent the body in nature but fuses both into one inseparable force, an elemental language of soil, flame, and flesh. In her leaves and silhouettes, the personal becomes archetypal, the temporary becomes timeless. Even in its small and delicate form, Untitled resonates as a profound meditation on belonging, memory, and the enduring power of the human spirit inscribed upon the earth.

provenance: Marlborough Fine Art Ltd., Vaduz | Private Collection, Geneva (acquired from the above in 1987) | Thence by descent to the present owner | | Exhibited | Munich, Kunsthalle der Hypo-Kulturstiftung, Fernando Botero: Bilder, Zeichnungen, Skulpturen, 4 July - 7 September 1986, no. 86 (illustrated n.p.) (and later travelled to Bremen, Kunsthalle Bremen, 11 January - 1 March 1987; Frankfurt, Schirn Kunsthalle Frankfurt, 12 March - 17 May 1987) | Madrid, Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, Fernando Botero: Pinturas, Dibujos, Esculturas, 22 June - 15 August 1987 (illustrated p. 96) | | | | A distilled expression of Fernando Botero's renowned figurative style, Muchacha from 1984, presents a young girl rendered with sculptural stability and candid existence. Standing frontally against a muted background, her distinct form is presented with gentle curves and compact proportions, giving the figure a sense of undeniable self-determination, despite the work's modest appearance. Botero deliberately restrains narrative, gesture, and expression, instead giving a self-contained presence to the figure, allowing his signature form and style to stand on its own. Unidealised and uninhibited in her representation, this young girl occupies her frame with unspoken authority, exemplifying Botero's commitment to form and volume as a force of presence, not drama or performance. Executed at the apex of the 'Maestro's' artistic maturity, Muchacha exemplifies the central role of works on paper in Botero's practice, where line and proportion articulate volume with a clarity and authority equal to his paintings and sculpture. | | Born in Medellín, in 1932, Botero undertook formative training in Madrid and Florence, where fascination with the works of the Old Masters profoundly shaped his approach to form, subject, and surface. Instead of functioning as a recreation or retelling, Muchacha acts as a synthesis of Botero's diverse influences. Flawless rosy skin and gently curving volumes take direction from the Renaissance's relationship to the body, yet Botero also echoes Flemish portraiture in the figure's frontal stance and emotional reserve. Subverting the western canon further, Muchacha reflects the grounding, compact nature of pre-Colombian figures, rejecting what he described the "anorexic" standards of European art, replacing idealisation with fullness, containment, and solidity. | | A recurring theme throughout many of Botero's works, the female form has always been a pertinent protagonist in his oeuvre. Muchacha's pink dress, heart shaped hair clip, and bouquet of flowers are all typical symbols of youthful femininity, but her form is diametrically opposed. Even in technique, Botero's use of buildable watercolour, rather than the strict opacity of oil, introduces a visual lightness that contrasts with the perceived weight and solidity of the form. Luminous skin tones and soft shadows temper mass with delicacy, reinforcing the tension between vulnerability and strength that animates the composition. Botero's deep examination of the conventions of art history allowed him to masterfully subvert expectations of the traditionally interlinked ideas of bodily form and self-expression. Affirming Botero's steadfast belief in separating physical embodiment from identity, Muchacha stands strong in her self-expression despite the artist's distortion. | | Executed in 1984, Muchacha emerged during a period of consolidation in Botero's artistic career. Moving to Italy with a new bronze-working studio one year earlier, his renewed commitment to sculpture is expertly reflected in the young girl's, solid, unmoving stance, serving as a translation of physical weight into a two-dimensional landscape. The work was prestigiously exhibited three years later in Madrid's Reina Sofia Museum in the artist's solo exhibition: Pinturas. Dibujos. Esculturas. This was Botero's his first major European retrospective that encompassed bronzes, paintings, and drawings. Presenting Muchacha alongside large portraits and re-interpretations of classical works, the exhibition exemplified the consistency and far-reaching scale of Botero's iconic visual language, as well as his positioning against broader shifts from the figurative towards the abstract in the 1980s avant-garde. Ultimately, Muchacha demonstrates a succinct articulation of Botero's matured visual language, where volume, restraint, and subversion converge to display the artist's mastery and understanding of visual expectation.

provenance: Marlborough Fine Art Ltd., London | Acquired from the above by the present owner in 2006 | | Exhibited | London, Marlborough Fine Art Ltd., Frank Auerbach: Recent Works, January – February 1997, no. 25 (illustrated n.p.) | | Literature | William Feaver, Frank Auerbach, New York, 2009, no. 773 (illustrated pp. 170 and 326) | William Feaver, Frank Auerbach, New York, 2022, no. 773 (illustrated pp. 172 and 368) | | | | Widely regarded as one of the most significant painters of post-war Britain, throughout his illustrious career Frank Auerbach sustained an uncompromising commitment to the creation of a raw and vital image derived from sustained observation of the seated model. The pursuit of this living presence, at once physical and psychological, remained central to his oeuvre. Renowned for the density and authority of his impasto, which powerfully structured and animated the pictorial surface, Auerbach produced some of the most compelling and materially ambitious portraits of the post-war period. His first solo exhibition was held at London's Beaux Arts Gallery in 1956, and in the decades that followed, his work became among the most widely collected and internationally exhibited of any contemporary British artist. Auerbach's approach to portraiture was shaped by a deep engagement with art history, from Rembrandt and Soutine to Giacometti and de Kooning, which informed both the material density of his surfaces and his existential understanding of the figure. | | Painted in 1996, Head of Catherine Lampert belongs to a sustained and intensely focused series of portraits of Catherine Lampert, Auerbach's close friend, biographer, and long-term sitter. The two first met in 1978, when Lampert was organising Auerbach's retrospective at the Hayward Gallery in London and conducted an extensive interview for the accompanying catalogue. Their professional relationship evolved into a profound artistic collaboration: Lampert later became Director of the Whitechapel Gallery in 1988 and curated Auerbach's major retrospective at the Royal Academy in 2001, further shaping the public and critical understanding of his work. Over decades, Lampert sat for Auerbach up to twice weekly, becoming the subject of more than seventy portraits. These works extended and deepened the serial investigations of the human head that had preoccupied the artist since the 1950s, following a lineage of sitters such as Stella West (E.O.W.), Juliet Yardley Mills (J.Y.M.), and his wife, Julia. Through repeated engagement, Auerbach pursued not conventional likeness, but a continually renewed encounter with the physical and psychological reality of the model. | | Head of Catherine Lampert demonstrates Auerbach's dialogue with sitter and tradition through a forceful orchestration of paint. The portrait reveals expressive brushwork and dense impasto, in which a vibrant amalgamation of colour and texture lends the surface an almost sculptural authority. Thickly layered pigment accumulates across the canvas, asserting the materiality of paint even as it forms a recognisable likeness. Lampert described the charged atmosphere of the studio: "Auerbach moves noisily around the room, looks at the painting in the mirror, turns the canvas, stands back, and then rushes up, and like darts or writing on the blackboard fairly brutally tries the next throw or cancels the previous one. He is continuously active, drawing in the air, talking to himself, hardly pausing." (Catherine Lampert, Frank Auerbach Paintings and Drawings 1954–2001, exh. cat. Royal Academy of Arts, London, 2001, p. 62). Her account underscores the physical and psychological intensity of Auerbach's process, an activity defined by constant revision and the gradual accumulation of knowledge about the sitter. | | Dominating the central right-hand passages of the composition in rich impasto, the thickly layered brushstrokes press forward, rising from areas where the paint has been applied with a faster, higher energy, producing a tension between figure and background that is synonymous with Auerbach's celebrated mark-making. Opulent reds, earthy browns, and vibrant yellows converge in a dense topography of pigment. Lampert's head emerges through swirling accumulation of brushstrokes, projecting with almost relief-like force, her facial features articulated through decisive strokes and daubs, each gesture carrying descriptive and expressive weight. Yet despite its material density, the portrait conveys a striking sense of temporal and psychological suspension: "that odd limbo, not an unpleasant state, of drifting from practical self-reminders into daydreams and unquantifiable desires." (Catherine Lampert in William Feaver, Frank Auerbach, New York, 2009, p. 21). | | Although fundamentally a figurative painter, the intensity and singularity of Auerbach's technique render his portraits essentially abstract, reflecting not only the sitter's physical presence but also the artist's emotional and psychological engagement. As Feaver observed, "Auerbach's heads are conceived not as busts or cameos but as presences" (William Feaver, ibid., p. 20), highlighting the existential immediacy of his figures. In Head of Catherine Lampert, his masterful use of colour and decisive painterly gestures conveys a powerful emotional charge, synthesising observation, material density, and psychological depth. Thus, the present work exemplifies Auerbach's inimitable approach to portraiture, in which the act of seeing, the physicality of paint, and the intimacy of human presence converge, producing a work of profound resonance and enduring significance in contemporary British art.

provenance: Private collection, Dordogne; their sale, Martinie Enchères, Brive-la-Gaillarde, 24 November 2018, lot 450. | Private collection, London (acquired at the above sale). | | | Henri Lebasque's Bord de Marne à Lagny belongs to one of the most fruitful and lyrical moments of the artist's career, when Lebasque, newly settled outside Paris for health reasons, immersed himself in the quiet rhythms of life along the banks of the Marne. Executed during his years in Lagny-sur-Marne, this work exemplifies Lebasque's deeply personal synthesis of Impressionist observation and post-Impressionist colour, resulting in a vision of nature suffused with light, serenity, and immediacy. | | | The composition unfolds with graceful assurance. On the left, a stand of trees rises from the riverbank, their trunks rendered not in naturalistic browns but in an animated spectrum of golds, ochres, blues and reds. Their branches arc gently over the water, framing the scene while guiding the eye across the shimmering surface of the river toward the distant village beyond. Lebasque's brushwork is lively and responsive: short, dappled strokes and cross-hatched touches dissolve form into reflection, allowing the water to act as both mirror and atmosphere. Mauves, pinks and soft purples articulate shadow and vibration, a distinctly Impressionist vocabulary used here with remarkable delicacy and control. | | | The chromatic range is dominated by cool blues and greens, enlivened by flashes of rose and pale gold, particularly along the horizon and within the river's reflective plane. These pastel-inflected tones, combined with Lebasque's use of atmospheric perspective, soften the distant banks and village houses, which are suggested with a few deft strokes. The sky, occupying the upper right quadrant, opens the composition outward: light clouds swirl across a pale expanse tinged with pink, reinforcing the sense of fleeting weather and a specific, transitory moment in time. | | | This emphasis on light, reflection, and the water's edge places the painting firmly within the central concerns of Impressionism, yet Lebasque's temperament distinguishes the work from that of his predecessors. While adapting the lessons of Monet, Renoir and Degas — particularly their plein-air practices and attention to optical sensation — Lebasque avoids bravura effects in favour of intimacy and calm. In this zone of contemplation, the river flows quietly, the village rests in the distance, and human presence is implied rather than asserted, reinforcing the harmony between landscape and lived experience. | | | The present work relates closely to Two Fishermen in a Boat on the Marne (1903), now in the collection of the Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza, a composition of similar scale and format painted during the same period. Both works demonstrate Lebasque's exploration of divisionist brushwork at this moment, a technique he would soon abandon, using finely articulated strokes to achieve extraordinary effects of light, transparency and reflection. Yet while the Thyssen painting introduces figures and a more enclosed framing, Bord de Marne à Lagny adopts a more expansive viewpoint. Here, the artist steps back, allowing greater prominence to the river's reflective surface and the open sky, resulting in a composition of heightened luminosity and spatial breadth. | | | Compared to the Thyssen work, the palette of the present painting is more highly keyed and vibrantly cool, suggesting a different moment of day or season — perhaps early morning or late afternoon in spring or early summer. The foliage appears fuller and more verdant, the blues richer and more varied, ranging from sapphire and turquoise to pale, silvery reflections. The reflection of the trees in the water is rendered with particular care, using tighter, more staccato strokes that lend the surface a crystalline clarity. These subtle distinctions underscore Lebasque's sensitivity to changing light and atmosphere, as well as his commitment to capturing nature as a living, mutable presence. | | | Lebasque's years along the Marne marked a period of consolidation and confidence. Influenced by Pissarro, Luce and Signac — whom he encountered at the Salon des Indépendants in the 1890s — he nonetheless resisted the rigidity of systematic Neo-Impressionism. As Denise Bazetoux observed, Lebasque sought above all to express his own vision of nature, one rooted in joy, balance, and a deeply felt response to the world around him. His landscapes from this time are imbued with what contemporaries recognised as a rare serenity, reflecting both the harmony of his personal life and his profound engagement with the subtleties of light in the Île-de-France. | | | Bord de Marne à Lagny stands as a compelling example of this achievement. At once observational and poetic, it captures the spirit of an artist at ease with his medium, translating the fleeting sensations of colour, weather and reflection into a composition of lasting freshness and grace. In this way, the painting encapsulates the quiet modernity of Lebasque's vision and his distinctive contribution to the evolution of French landscape painting at the turn of the twentieth century.

artwork_title: Les arbres sur la rive, Quimperlé
provenance: Galerie J. Allard, Paris (acquired directly from the artist). | Anon. sale, Hôtel Drouot, Paris, 6 March 1967, lot 14. | Mr & Mrs James R. Holland Collection, New York (acquired at the above sale); their sale, Peachtree & Bennett, Atlanta, 11 October 2014, lot 16. | Private collection, UK (acquired at the above sale). | | Exhibited | Brussels, Galerie des Artistes Français, Le Sidaner, October - November 1931, no. 35 (titled 'Les arbres de la rive'). | | Literature | Y. Farinaux-Le Sidaner, Le Sidaner, L'oeuvre peint et gravé, Paris, 1989, no. 704 (illustrated p. 258). | | | Born on the island of Mauritius, and the son of a long-distance sea captain who disappeared at sea, Henri Le Sidaner grew up in Dunkirk, a northern port city defined by its harbours and tides. Surrounded from an early age by an element that would become a leitmotiv of his artistic practice, water left a lasting imprint on the artist's memory and imagination. Its never-ending capacity for reflective stillness and mesmerising, perpetually shifting reflections became deeply embedded in the artist's memory and imagination, and throughout his career Le Sidaner returned persistently to ports, canals and quiet waterways, making them central subjects of his oeuvre. The present work, Les arbres sur la rive, Quimperlé, stands within this lifelong meditation on water and its poetic resonance. | | Painted in his Versailles studio in 1931, the composition is inspired by the artist's memory of Quimperlé, a modest Breton town situated at the confluence of three rivers, which the artist had visited several years earlier. Working from sketches he had made when he was in Quimperlé, Le Sidaner recreated the scene guided by memory and sensation, likely influenced by important port scenes such as Claude Gellée's (Le Lorrain) Seaport (1644). With its golden light, classical architecture and tranquil water, Claude's celebrated painting similarly transforms a natural landscape into a poetic meditation on atmosphere and stillness — anticipating the quiet, contemplative mood that Le Sidaner would later evoke through his more intimate, Symbolist-inflected handling of light and space. | | Les arbres sur la rive, Quimperlé is set at the end of a sunny day. A hushed luminosity suffuses the scene, wherein vertical trunks rise like quiet sentinels before a canal. The composition is governed by a rhythmic alternation of upright lines and receding space: the trees, evenly spaced along the riverbank, create a measured cadence whose silence is only disrupted by the gentle diagonals of the boats' masts, suggesting the soft, hollow echoes of the boats' hulls as they are lulled by the water. | | The long shadows of the trees, rendered with an almost pointillist sensibility, recall Camille Pissarro's sun-drenched Late Afternoon in Our Meadow (1887), which shares similar tones of muted mauve, powdery blue and pink, and warm yellow on the ground, with small trees casting longer shadows than their height would suggest. These long silhouettes recall the hands of a sundial and suggest at once the passage of time and its slow, unhurried movement, evoking late sunny afternoons that seem to stretch endlessly beneath a generous, lingering light. The elongated trees and the sinuous line they follow along the riverbank, giving the composition a dynamic perspective that draws the eye inward, also recall Claude Monet's Poplars (Autumn) (1891), which shares a similar autumnal light. | | In Les arbres sur la rive, Quimperlé, different colours dissolve into one another in a tapestry of vibrant brushstrokes. The foliage above shimmers with touches of rose, gold and ochre, suggesting autumnal light filtered through leaves rather than sharp contrasts. The canal itself is rendered in softened reflections, its surface a veil of turquoise and pale jade that echoes the shadows on the ground. Creating a mosaic-like surface, Le Sidaner masterfully illustrates light through chromatic vibrancy, with an 'extremely varied and subtle [palette] [...] [where] the oils bind and melt together in delicate harmonies. [...] With him, contours seem to emerge from the interplay of light, and in this respect, he is similar to Claude Monet'. (J. Baschet in L'Illustration, 1924, quoted in Y. Farinaux-Le Sidaner, Le Sidaner, L'oeuvre peint et gravé, Paris, 1989, p. 37). | | Le Sidaner held the Impressionists and Claude Monet in deep admiration, writing that the latter was '[working] to conquer a new light every day.' (H. Le Sidaner, De la lumiere et de la couleur, 1935, quoted in Y. Farinaux-Le Sidaner, op. cit., p. 34). Indeed, for the Impressionists the work was never done, as light constantly changes. One of the most telling examples of this was Claude Monet's quasi-scientific observation of daylight on the same building at different times of day in his Rouen Cathedral series (1892–1894). Le Sidaner pursued this same obsession, which led some critics to say that 'in the past, he seemed to proceed as an Impressionist, painting light on surfaces rather than surfaces themselves' (C. Mauclair, Preface to the catalogue of the Georges Petit exhibition, 1935, quoted in Y. Farinaux-Le Sidaner, op. cit., p. 39). In fact, the light in Les arbres sur la rive, Quimperlé is not so different from that in Monet's Cathédrale de Rouen, Effet de soleil (Fin de journée) (1892), painted at the end of a sunny day. | | In deliberate contrast to the Impressionists, Le Sidaner did not habitually complete his paintings en plein air. Instead, he worked in the studio from sketches made on site and from memory once he had returned home. By distancing himself from direct observation, he freed his compositions from the burden of reality and reshaped the scenes through the filter of memory and sensation. As Camille Mauclair observed, Le Sidaner '[retained] the finest principles of the Impressionist masters in order to employ them in the expression of a psychological ideal altogether different from realism' (C. Mauclair, L'Impressionisme, Son histoire, son esthétique, ses maîtres, Paris, 1904, p. 198). In this way, his painting becomes less an exercise in empirical truth than an act of poetic reconstruction, where memory mediates perception and atmosphere supersedes fact. | | In the paintings of Henri Le Sidaner, human figures are rare, and when they do appear, they are more suggested than truly seen. Here, in a quiet and uncommon moment, a fisherman stands at the centre left, tidying his tools aboard his boat at the end of a day's work. His presence does not dominate the scene; he is barely more than a shadow, almost dissolving into the surrounding light. This absence of clearly defined figures deepens the contemplative mood of the work. The painting feels suspended — poised delicately between reality and reverie — and becomes less a depiction of place than an evocation of atmosphere: a quiet meditation in colour, where light and water captivate the viewer in an instant of reverie. This introspective view, created from memory and old sketches, situates Le Sidaner at a mesmerising intersection between Impressionism and Symbolism. | | Indeed, the painting resists narrative closure. No event unfolds, no figure commands interpretation; instead, meaning arises from the subtle orchestration of stillness. Le Sidaner thus moves away from Impressionism and its objectivity towards Symbolism and its emphasis on mood, suggestion, and inner experience rather than clear narrative. This softly lit landscape feels less like a specific location and more like a poetic evocation of solitude and reverie at the end of a quiet afternoon, reminiscent of Debussy's Prélude à l'Après-midi d'un faune (1892–1894). Both compositions avoid traditional development, dissolve sharp outlines, and create an atmosphere of suspension and introspection in a late sunny afternoon of natural contemplation, thus privileging sensation and the evocative power of suggestion over literal representation. | | In the words of Paul Signac, Le Sidaner was 'a master at creating tender, soft, and silent atmospheres' (P. Signac quoted in Y. Farinaux-Le Sidaner, op. cit., p. 31). Offering a wonderful sentimental evocation of the landscape, Les arbres sur la rive, Quimperlé stands as a compelling example of Le Sidaner's elegiac tone, situating the spectator within the scene, as though standing quietly among the trees, absorbed in solitary contemplation for a moment of respite, at a time when much of European art pursued fragmentation, political engagement, or radical formal experimentation.

provenance: Gift from the artist to the present owner | | Exhibited | London, Gagosian Gallery, Britannia Street, Damien Hirst: The Complete Spot Paintings 1986-2011, 12 January - 18 February 2012 | | Literature | Jason Beard & Millicent Wilner (eds.), Damien Hirst: The Complete Spot Paintings 1986-2011, London, 2013 (illustrated p. 84) | | | | Executed in 1994,  Argininamine represents an early iteration of the body of work that propelled Damien Hirst to international prominence and critical distinction. Comprised of one hundred and fifty-six meticulously arranged, uniquely coloured dots set in a precise matrix of twelve rows and thirteen columns, Argininamine stands as an early and important example of Damien Hirst's acclaimed Spot series. Each chromatic sphere, while uniform in scale and spatial placement, is distinguished by its individual hue, creating a composition that is both systematically ordered and visually diverse. Despite the potential for infinite permutations within this framework, the overarching themes of life, death, science and art, and conceptual undercurrents resonate consistently throughout the entire series. With a diversely hued palette and distinct composition, Argininamine demonstrates these core principles with a high degree of formal control and precision. | | Emerging as a central figure among the Young British Artists during the late 1980s and 1990s, Hirst and his contemporaries were characterised by an entrepreneurial spirit and an embrace of unconventional, often provocative materials and methods. His first curatorial initiative, Freeze - staged in 1988 while he was still a student at Goldsmiths College of Art - featured two Spot paintings and marked a pivotal moment, catalysing the rise of both Hirst and the YBA collective to immediate recognition within the contemporary art world. Each spot in the series is painstakingly executed by hand using household gloss paint within a rigorously predetermined grid, a practice that interrogates the tension between mechanical precision and the corporeal trace of human intervention. | | Argininamine is part of the most well-known subseries of the Spot series; the Pharmaceutical paintings. These were initially conceived alongside Hirst's renowned Medicine Cabinets and further the artist's lifelong interest in the conversation between faith, art and science. Hirst sees medicine as a potent belief system, in which society is seduced by drugs and persuaded of their capacity to cure all ailments and sustain life, while rarely interrogating their side effects: "Art is like medicine, it can heal. Yet I've always been amazed at how many people believe in medicine but don't believe in art" (D. Hirst, I want to spend the rest of my life everywhere, with everyone, one to one, always, forever, now, London 2006, p. 246). The artist derived the titles of each Pharmaceutical painting from an alphabetical listing of drug names cited in the Sigma-Aldrich chemical company catalogue that he first encountered in the early 1990s. As such, the Pharmaceutical paintings can be seen as an extension of the medical supplies found in Hirst's Medicine Cabinets with each spot signifying an individual pill. | | Through each carefully hand-painted spot, Hirst is able to establish his broader artistic philosophy while creating a distinctive and instantly recognizable visual language. The artist has built upon this discourse over the years, creating a triumphant output of fully unique works that utilize this language. Entirely fresh to the market, Argininamine was included in Gagosian Gallery's ambitious 2012 exhibition series The Complete Spot Paintings 1986–2011, which presented over 300 works from the series across all eleven of the gallery's global locations. Spanning a remarkable range in scale — from minuscule pinhole-sized marks to expansive compositions featuring spots measuring up to 60 inches in diameter — each spot asserts a presence that becomes acutely palpable when viewed in person. This singular exhibition series highlighted the artist's impressive production and investigation of the spot, which is central to Hirst's aesthetic inquiry exploring the dialectic between seriality and individuality. As he reflects: "I've always liked series. [...] You get some sort of security from the repetition of a series. If you say something twice, it's pretty convincing. It's more convincing than if you say it once. I think it's also the implication of the endlessness, which kind of theoretically helps you avoid death. [...] People are afraid of change, so you create a kind of belief for them through repetition. It's like breathing. So I've always been drawn to series and pairs. A unique thing is quite a frightening object" (The artist in conversation with Hans Ulrich Obrist, In the darkest hour there might be light: Works from Damien Hirst's Murderme Collection, London, Serpentine Gallery/Other Criteria, 2008). | | Unfolding across a radiant chromatic spectrum, Argininamine  manifests a structured, contemplative grid that invites reflection on the intricate interrelations among science, religion, art, beauty, life, and death. As resonant today as at the time of its creation, this work offers a powerful, lyrical meditation on themes that remain central to the human condition. Through its elegant synthesis of order and emotion, Argininamine epitomises Hirst's enduring engagement with existential inquiry and aesthetic precision.

provenance: Sadie Coles HQ, London | Acquired from the above by the present owner in 2016 | | Exhibited | Venice, The British Pavillion, 56th Venice International Art Biennale, I SCREAM DADDIO, 9 May - 22 November 2015 (another from the edition exhibited and illustrated pp. 91, 93 and 94) | | Illustrated images are of another work from the edition. | | | | Executed in 2015, Sarah Lucas' Gold Cup Maradona is exuberant, monumental and commands attention through its scale, colour, and complex composition. Distinctive within the artist's oeuvre for its imposing size, the present work bears the hallmarks of Lucas' internationally acclaimed work. The result is a striking sculpture that perfectly epitomises the artist's decades-long rebellious yet playful engagement with the art historical tradition of the portrayal of the human form, challenging traditional notions of gender, sexuality and identity. Through its twists and bulges, the present work depicts an anthropomorphic cast whose natural bodily contours mirror and reshape reality. With Gold Cup Maradona, Lucas elevates bravado and bodily excess to an epic status, gleaming with irreverence and audacity. | | First presented on the portico of the British Pavilion at the 56th Venice Biennale in 2015, Gold Cup Maradona asserts both physical and conceptual dominance. Originally conceived specifically for this site, the sculpture exemplifies Lucas' long-standing commitment to creating work in direct and thoughtful dialogue with its surroundings. During its Venice presentation, the boldly masculine, fluid contours of Gold Cup Maradona sprawled across the British Pavilion's entrance, dynamically disrupting the restraint of its neoclassical façade while simultaneously enticing viewers into the pavilion by provoking curiosity through its irreverent presence. The figure's towering phallus audaciously sliced through the Gran Bretagna sign, yet this irreverent act was accompanied by a thoughtful engagement with art history: the sculpture occupied the same site as Henry Moore's Double Standing Figure in 1948. Here, Lucas established a purposeful challenge between the comical representation of the sexualised male form and Moore's abstract figures, which intended to represent the optimistic and humanist values embodied in modernism. Notably, at the time of the 56th Venice Biennale, only four women prior to Lucas had been selected to exhibit in the British Pavilion: Barbara Hepworth in 1950, Bridget Riley in 1968, Rachel Whiteread in 1997, and Tracey Emin in 2007. As such, the commanding sculpture that greeted visitors served as a powerful articulation of Lucas' mature confidence in her position as a leading British female artist at the time of the work's creation, a distinction that the artist still carries today. | | Lucas is widely associated with sculptural depictions of the female body fashioned from soft fabrics and pliable materials – most notably tights, which openly allude to conventionally feminine objects and rituals. Gold Cup Maradona, by contrast, turns to the male form and to bronze, a resolute and weighty material often coded as robust or even masculine. Yet through this medium Lucas deftly conjures a sense of bodily suppleness, lending the sculpture an inviting tactility and warmth that temper its imposing presence despite the material's inherent hardness. In doing so, the work conveys a delicacy and vulnerability comparable to that found in her fabric-based pieces. This portrayal of the male body, poised between figurative abstraction and sexualised formalisation, carries a palpable vitality and fragility akin to that sensed in the artist's flexible textile sculptures. | | The choice of yellow is reminiscent of Lucas' recurring engagement with eggs, evident throughout her practice, where these function both as humorous references to the female body and as symbols of fertility and reproduction. One of the most recognisable works by the artist is Self Portrait with Fried Eggs, from 1996, where two fried eggs were placed on the artist's breasts as a playful representation of femininity and fertility while defying common representations of women through the male gaze. The incorporation of eggs throughout the artist's practice "put[s] the fate of the egg – typically understood as the female reproductive cell – into the hands of women, perhaps alluding to political debates concerning women's rights over their own bodies" (Margot Norton, Sarah Lucas Au Naturel, New York 2019 p. 99). As Lucas herself explains, "So why yellow? Is it because I've been wondering, in terms of the two large sculptures, what colour they should be? Or is [it] because I've been wondering how to get eggs into the thing?" (S. Lucas, I SCREAM DADDIO, London, 2015, p. 52). Lucas experimented extensively with different shades of yellow, testing them on various surfaces and observing how they shifted under changing light conditions and at different times of day. Ultimately, the artist chose a colour called Gold Cup, a vivid yellow, for the present work, exhibited on the outside of the pavilion, and Deep Cream, a slightly paler variation, for its sister-piece exhibited inside, with each colour contributing its name to the work's title. | | Renowned for her bold, mischievous, and unapologetically provocative approach, Lucas' practice is defined by irreverent humour and the inventive use of visual puns and crude euphemisms. Working across sculpture, photography, and installation, her work consistently engages the body in its physical, cultural, and psychological dimensions. With both wit and sincerity, Lucas addresses themes of sex, mortality, and British identity, embracing sensationalism as a strategic and critical tool rather than mere shock. Her suggestive forms deftly undermine clichés propagated by popular media, while her sustained interrogation of gender foregrounds the performative nature of femininity and masculinity. Gold Cup Maradona stands as a confident and celebratory culmination of Sarah Lucas' sculptural prowess, uniting humour, provocation, and historical awareness within its fluid, imposing and striking forms. Through its monumental scale, radiant colour, and deliberate engagement with site and gender representations, the present work asserts Lucas' authoritative voice within British and international contemporary art, leaving an enduring and unforgettable impression on both the pavilion and its viewers alike. | |

provenance: Gift from the artist to the present owner | | | | Executed circa 1995, Beautiful, Dental, Brushing, Full Mouth Rehabilitation, Thank You Painting is an early and luminous example of Damien Hirst's iconic series of Spin paintings. Hirst initiated this body of work in 1992, experimenting with the centrifugal force of a rapidly rotating circular canvas onto which he poured vivid streams of household paint. These celebrated Spin paintings captivate through their vibrant kineticism, generated by the spontaneous operations of chance, as the artist's own hand is nearly removed from the final composition. The methodology of the present work recalls Jackson Pollock's revolutionary drip paintings, through which Pollock pioneered a technique of dynamically dripping and pouring skeins of paint onto canvas or paper spread upon the floor beneath him. Similarly animated and bursting with chromatic intensity that seems to extend beyond the canvas's perimeter, Hirst's Spin paintings engage the uncertainty inherent in human experience, emblematic of the artist's enduring pursuit to transcend predetermined limits within his own artistic practice. | | Shaped by postmodernism's privileging of chance and the aleatory, Hirst's Spin paintings stand in marked contrast to his methodical Spot series, though both interrogate the notion of an imagined mechanical artist, which is a conceit Hirst has provocatively sustained throughout his diverse oeuvre. Beautiful, Dental, Brushing, Full Mouth Rehabilitation, Thank You Painting unites the automatic with the tactile, creating organic, unique painterly gestures through a regulated process. The tension between automation and chance lies at the heart of Hirst's practice, through which he seeks to unsettle convention and extend the formal and conceptual boundaries of painting, while reaffirming his enduring engagement with mortality, where chance and control remain inextricably entwined. | | As with much of Hirst's oeuvre, the apparent simplicity of the spin painting technique is inseparable from his fundamental interrogation of art's function and value. The artist has recounted that the series was inspired by childhood memories of watching Blue Peter presenter John Noakes demonstrate a variant of the process using a motorised cardboard spinning device. Some time after viewing the broadcast, Hirst attended a school event where he first attempted spin painting himself, recalling a sustained fascination and near-obsessive compulsion to repeat the act again and again. Ironically, Hirst later inaugurated his own spin painting enterprise within a comparable milieu: after producing several early works in his Brixton studio in 1992, he established, the following year, a spin art stall with fellow artist Angus Fairhurst at Joshua Compston's street fair A Fête Worse than Death. For the occasion, the performance artist Leigh Bowery famously transformed Hirst and Fairhurst into clowns, and visitors were invited to produce their own spin paintings, which the artists signed upon completion. | | In 1994, whilst living in Berlin, Hirst commissioned the fabrication of his own spin machine, a development that marked the moment at which the series began to take shape. Created circa 1995, the present work encapsulates the euphoric ecstasy of these early investigations. As the Spin paintings became increasingly popular, Hirst never lost his childlike sense of wonder in the process that had inspired him as a young boy. It remained, for him, 'a miracle of technology'; 'I really like making them', he professed. 'And I really like the machine, and I really like the movement. Every time they're finished, I'm desperate to do another one' (D. Hirst, quoted in D. Hirst and G. Burn, On the Way to Work, London 2001, p. 221). Ultimately, these works function as unrestrained affirmations of the power of painting: by removing his own hand directly from the process, Hirst reawakens a primal sense of awe in its unpredictable possibilities. | | Hypnotic in composition and resplendent in chromatic brilliance, Beautiful, Dental, Brushing, Full Mouth Rehabilitation, Thank You Painting is an exquisitely executed work that provides a kaleidoscopic and meditative experience for the viewer. |

provenance: Galerie Durant-Dessert, Paris | Private Collection, France (acquired from the above in 1989) | Anon. sale, Sotheby's, New York, 12 May 2016, lot 139 | Acquired from the above by the present owner | | Literature | Exh. cat., Alighiero Boetti, Ravenna, 1984, no. 7 (illustrated pp. 44-45) | Bernard Blistène, 'Fontana Burri Manzoni e l'Arte Povera: La Mauvaise Question', in Artstudio, No. 13, Summer 1989 (illustrated p. 27) | Martin De Luca & Massimo Minimmi (eds.), Alighiero e Boetti, Ravenna, 1990, no. 46, p. 55 | Mark Kremmer, 'Lightness as a Weapon. On the Work of Alighiero e Boetti', in Archis, No. 2, February 1995 (illustrated p. 71) | Lara Vinca Masini, Arte Contemporanea, La Linea del Modello, Arte Come Progetto del Mondo, Florence, 1996, no. 3136 (illustrated p. 617) | Jean-Christophe Ammann, Alighiero Boetti, Catalogo generale, Tomo secondo, Opere 1972-1979, Milan, 2012, no. 951 (illustrated p. 287) | | | | Mettere i verbi all'infinito, from 1978, is a defining work from Alighiero Boetti's celebrated lavori biro series (or ballpoint drawings), which examine the intersections of linguistic, numerical and visual systems. Initiated in 1972, the series employs the modest medium of the ballpoint pen to generate densely textured fields of colour, composed of accumulative strokes and punctuated by small, luminous white commas. Through this controlled yet open-ended process, Mettere i verbi all'infinito beautifully articulates Boetti's sustained engagement with structure, language, systematisation and the production of meaning. | | Though seemingly dispersed randomly across the page, each comma is meticulously positioned to correspond with a specific letter of the alphabet, identifiable by tracing their sequence against the key along the left-hand side of the composition. As Boetti explained, "A word turns into a sign, into a compilation of commas with a meaning... you must render the comma as something that is not stable" (the artist quoted in Alighiero Boetti: Mettere al mondo il mondo, Frankfurt, 1998, p. 63). Moving from left to right, the viewer gradually deciphers the coded message, which in this instance reveals the title: Mettere i verbi all'infinito. In engaging the viewer in this process of revelation, Boetti constructs a subtle yet playful game that simultaneously deconstructs and celebrates the capacity of letters to convey information, while poetically acknowledging his enduring fascination with language and wordplay. The work destabilises the perceived authority of the Latin alphabet, exposing it as an artificial system governed by arbitrary rules rather than a fixed conduit of meaning. In doing so, it evokes a sustained tension between control and uncertainty, logic and intuition, as comprehension emerges incrementally through careful attention. This delicate oscillation between order and unpredictability exemplifies one of Boetti's central preoccupations: ordine e disordine, opposing forces that coexist in a state of continual flux, shaping the conceptual framework of his practice. | | Made up of three individual panels, each painstakingly filled with rich, subtly gradated fields of royal blue ink, Mettere i verbi all'infinito presents a shimmering vision of space, the white commas appearing like a mysterious astronomical constellation or a series of falling raindrops against its expanse. While the laborious process demanded a heightened level of attention to ensure the surface was filled as densely as possible, a number of subtle textural shifts can be detected throughout. Each panel is imbued with the distinctive rhythm of its maker, resulting in fluctuating fields of colour that appear to undulate across the composition. These variations depend on numerous factors: from the quality of the pen and the pressure applied, to the speed of each stroke, the temperament of the maker, and even the gradual loss of pigment as the pen began to run out of ink. | | In each of the lavori biro works, Boetti employed a group of collaborators to realise his vision. While the artist developed the concept and defined the basic grid pattern, the execution of the composition was entrusted to others. A similar method was used in the artist's Arazzi and Mappe series, both of which relied on the technical skills of Afghan embroiderers. By adopting this process, Boetti established a form of relational aesthetics through which he explored the role of the artist as a conceiver rather than the sole creator of a work of art. In the case of the biro drawings, he drew assistants from his local neighbourhood of Trastevere in Rome and requested that each alternating panel be coloured by a member of the opposite sex. Armed with a clearly defined set of rules, his collaborators spent countless hours filling the panels with intricate layers of cross-hatching, a time-intensive process Boetti felt was intrinsic to the nature of the works: "The drawings in Biro are concentrates of time" (the artist quoted ibid, p. 59). | | This embrace of systems tempered by chance situates Mettere i verbi all'infinito in dialogue with the conceptual framework of Arte Povera, with which Boetti was closely associated in the late 1960s. Despite its materially modest components, everyday ballpoint pens and the labour of non-professional collaborators, the work extends beyond the movement's emphasis on physicality and process. Boetti redirects Arte Povera's anti-hierarchical ethos toward immaterial systems of language, time, and collective authorship. While resonating with the movement's resistance to industrialisation, commodification, and rigid formalism; the lavori biro depart from its material focus, privileging conceptual structures and delegated production as instruments for interrogating authorship and meaning. The visible traces of labour, the openness to error, and the gradual accumulation of ink, function not merely as evidence of process, but as markers of a philosophical inquiry that surpasses the movement's original scope. | | Executed in the 1970s, a decade that consolidated Boetti's conceptual interests, Mettere i verbi all'infinito emerges from a broader exploration of systems as both formal frameworks and metaphors for ordering the world. During this period, Boetti developed parallel bodies of work, most notably the Mappe, which charted geopolitical change, while also formalising his fascination with duality through the adoption of his doubled name, Alighiero e Boetti. Across these projects, he mobilised language, cartography, and delegated labour as interrelated strategies for examining authorship and temporality, holding structure and unpredictability in deliberate tension. In bringing these concerns together, Boetti's practice reflects an enduring interest in how meaning is shaped through processes that exceed individual intention. | | Mettere i verbi all'infinito transforms a deceptively simple system into a work of profound complexity and elegance. It exemplifies Boetti's capacity to balance conceptual rigor with chance and human variation, producing a composition that is simultaneously intellectually exacting and visually compelling. In its quiet complexity, Mettere i verbi all'infinito stands as a powerful testament to Boetti's ingenuity.

Tàpies, Madrid, 1990, Vol. IX, no. 12 (illustrated p. 28 and p. 86) | Anna Agustí, Tàpies, The Complete Works, Volume 3: 1969-1975, Barcelona, 1992, no. 2108 (illustrated p. 103) | | | | Precarious at first sight yet profoundly sophisticated in conception, Caixa d'embalar is a thought-provoking example of Antoni Tàpies' celebrated "matter paintings," affirming the artist's sustained commitment to the reinvention of painting and its expressive possibilities. Executed in 1969, the work bears the hallmarks of Tàpies' mature practice: densely worked, tactile surfaces constructed from humble, unconventional materials, in which form emerges through processes of accretion, abrasion, and concealment. Suspended between painting and object, Caixa d'embalar unfolds as a charged material terrain, its weathered surface evoking sedimented memory and the passage of time. Here, the ordinary packing case is transformed into a poetic field of enquiry, where matter itself functions as both subject and signifier. | | Initially indebted to the imaginative vocabularies of Surrealism, particularly those of Max Ernst, Joan Miró, and Paul Klee, Tàpies soon redirected his practice toward abstraction, first exploring restrained geometrical compositions before arriving at the radically tactile language that would define his mature production. By the early 1950s, and increasingly in the following decade, he aligned himself with the broader currents of Art Informel, forging a distinctly personal mode of "material abstraction" in which substance became both medium and message. In dialogue with contemporaries such as Jean Dubuffet and Alberto Burri, Tàpies rejected illusionistic depth in favour of surfaces activated through physical intervention; built up through sand, marble dust, wood, and discarded matter, then incised, scratched, or scored in gestures that evoke both violence and revelation. | | This dialectic of addition and subtraction, of concealment and exposure, finds eloquent expression in Caixa d'embalar. Layered sections emerge and recede across the packing case's worn façade, its rough-hewn edges and embedded fragments generating a palpable sense of sedimented time. The surface reads less as a pictorial field than as an archaeological site, bearing traces of process, touch, and human presence. Such material density underscores Tàpies' conviction that texture constituted a "third language," equal in expressive force to colour and form. For the artist, matter was never inert; it functioned as a conduit to metaphysical awareness. As he reflected, his works sought to create "a system that makes it possible to change the spectator's way of looking and to bring him or her closer to a state of contemplation of reality at its deepest level," enabling the perception of hidden depths and "inner illumination" (the artist quoted in: The UNESCO Courier, June 1994, p. 5). | | Tàpies' engagement with matter during the 1960s can further be understood within the broader context of contemporary material explorations in Europe and the United States. The emergence of Arte Povera in Italy and the parallel developments of Post-Minimalism and Process Art signalled a decisive shift away from the autonomy of the pristine art object toward practices grounded in contingency, entropy, and the poetics of the everyday. While Tàpies' material investigations predate these movements, they resonate profoundly with their concerns. In post-war Spain, and amid social, political, and cultural upheaval, matter assumed existential significance. As author Youssef Ishaghpour has observed, Tàpies sought to "confront the disillusionment and the absence of meaning in the obtuse force of matter" (Y. Ishaghpour, Antoni Tàpies, Barcelona, 2006, p. 56). Such historical and material conditions are legibly inscribed in Caixa d'embalar, whose worn timber, frayed fibres, and humble fragments evoke a world shaped by scarcity, rupture, and reconstruction, while asserting the resilience embedded within matter itself. | | The work's construction is particularly resonant as Tàpies incorporates a recycled packing box together with collaged elements of wood, straw, and paper, preserving the traces of labour and touch that cling to their surfaces. In doing so, he advances a conception of form not as abstract geometry but as lived substance, imbued with the memory of prior existence. These quotidian elements, dislodged from their utilitarian function, acquire symbolic charge and form both the structural and conceptual core of the work, recalling the enigmatic letters and signs of his canvases. By substituting the traditional canvas for a packing box, Tàpies transforms an object of transit and containment into a site of contemplation. Its hollow interior and abraded surfaces resist hierarchical composition, rejecting any singular focal point or fixed declaration of meaning and instead inviting the viewer to reconsider the ontological status of ordinary matter. | | This reconfiguration of the box as both structure and symbol also establishes the work's central material tensions. Caixa d'embalar articulates a dialogue between opposites: rigid, sharp-edged fragments of wood are set against soft, fragile straw and paper, which spill, press, and nestle within the crate's interior. The contrast between hardness and delicacy extends the earlier transformation of the packing box, foregrounding the agency of matter and allowing it to assert a palpable vitality. Even the sporadic application of paint, seemingly thrown across the surface, reinforces this dynamic, exemplifying Tàpies' equilibrium between controlled intervention and spontaneous gesture. In this balance, the fractured material realities of post-war Europe, marked by destruction, scarcity, and reconstruction, find quiet resonance. By permitting the ephemeral and the enduring to coexist within a single, unstable structure, the work becomes a meditation on resilience and impermanence, resisting narrative closure while inviting sustained, contemplative engagement with its surfaces and the histories they embody. | | Caixa d'embalar stands as a distilled expression of Tàpies' sustained exploration of matter, spirituality, and the boundaries of painting. By elevating a discarded packing box into a space for aesthetic and metaphysical reflection, he demonstrates painting's capacity to move beyond representation, functioning as an experiential field shaped by perception and tactility. The work's layered construction, the tension between fragility and resilience, and the visible traces of human intervention coalesce into an object that is at once concrete and contemplative, surface and depth intertwined. Here, the ordinary is neither obscured nor idealised, but intensified: matter speaks on its own terms, carrying the weight of history, touch, and time. Within the trajectory of Tàpies' mature practice, the work embodies the principles that mark his most significant contributions, material abstraction as philosophical enquiry, process as revelation, and the transformation of the everyday into the profound. In doing so, Caixa d'embalar emerges not merely as an example of his practice, but as a definitive statement of its enduring resonance in post-war European art.

provenance: Opera Gallery, Monaco | Acquired from the above by the present owner | | | | Manolo Valdés occupies a unique position in postwar European art; an archeologist of mythologies who reveals the tension between historical and contemporary spectacle, examining and producing art that engages deeply with the sociocultural potentialities of image-making and iconography. In the present work, Reina Mariana, Valdés' vision crystalises in a reanimated silhouette of the Spanish Golden Age. Lucent and amethyst-like, it presents as an object of nature – a piece derived from natural creation and order. Sublimated in this idea is the crux of Valdés' project: to upend the ideologies embedded in images of power. | | Emerging during the final decades of the Franco regime in Spain, for Valdés and his artistic comrades art was a vehicle for critique and cultural reclamation. A founding member of the Equipo Crónica in 1965, alongside Rafael Solbes and Juan Antonio Toledo, the group approached art history as an active archive, reconstituting images belonging to the Spanish tradition as a form of Pop art inflected through a politicized lens. "We used 'pop' but questioned it. We took the images (language) but knew it had to be different from the United States. We felt that American pop lacked the political content [...] We relied heavily on historical painting, which we converted into pop. For us the Museo del Prado represented the utmost expression of popular culture. Its contents became our main source of inspiration" (the artist quoted in: "Artist interview: Manolo Valdés (Equipo Crónica)", Tate, September 2015, Online). | | By reworking canonical paintings alongside comic-strip graphics and contemporary political imagery, Equipo Crónica exposed how cultural authority is imposed and disseminated. Their project was neither parody nor homage, but a critical investigation into how images accumulate meaning through repetition and institutional framing. After the dissolution of the collective in 1981 following the death of Solbes, this sustained dialogue with art history has been the driving force of Valdés' own practice, reenvisioning the works of Velázquez, repurposing the tools of Picasso and Matisse, Cubism and the Fauves. | | The present work employs Valdés' most prominent leitmotif, taking one of the most recognisable images of Spanish court painting, Velázquez's own 1652–1653 Portrait of Mariana of Austria – in the collection of the Museo del Prado – as it's departure point. The domed features of the subject's extravagant coiffure and architectural dress are inseparable from the work of Valdés. In his stripping of identity from the original image, Valdés emphasises collective memory over biography; the figure becomes less a historical person than a cultural symbol. | | Reina Mariana embodies a worldview that remains in living memory for Spain: history is neither neutral nor passive but is continuously reconstructed; that absolute power corrupts absolutely. The translation of a Baroque royal portrait into a contemporary sculpture demonstrates a fluidity at the heart of image-making. In its immaculate surface Reina Mariana conceals the hand of the artist, reaffirming the mediated perfection of reproduced images but also the natural order implied by autonomous, inhuman objects. Part-sculpture, part-monument, the present work is an elegant window through which the spectator glimpses the essential transparency of images that seek to project power or fortify ideology. | | Valdés has long since achieved global stardom and institutional acclaim, his sculptures appearing in public spaces of major cities around the world for decades, most notably representing Spain at the 48th Venice Biennale in 1999, and in 2006 being honored by the Museo Reina Sofía with a comprehensive career survey. There is little doubt in his international standing as an artist who has produced one of the most consistent and compelling bodies of work to emerge from Spain in the latter half of the 20th century.

Le Normand-Romain, The Bronzes of Rodin, Catalogue of Works in the Musée Rodin, Vol. I, Paris, 2007, pp. 335-337 (another cast illustrated p. 334; terracotta version illustrated p. 335; plaster version illustrated p. 336; marble versions illustrated pp. 336 & 337). | | One of Auguste Rodin's most celebrated sculptures and among the greatest commercial successes of his career, Eternal printemps was conceived in 1884 at a moment of profound emotional and artistic intensity. The work emerged during Rodin's passionate relationship with Camille Claudel, who had recently joined his studio as an assistant and whose presence would prove transformative to his art. Originally developed as part of La porte de l'Enfer — the monumental bronze doors inspired by Dante Alighieri's Inferno, commissioned in 1880 — the rapturous embrace of the lovers was ultimately deemed too hopeful in tone for Rodin's vision of damnation and despair. Freed from that context, Eternal printemps evolved into an autonomous celebration of desire, vitality and enduring passion. | | The entwined figures evoke the tragic lovers Paolo and Francesca, condemned in Dante's narrative to an eternity of wind-tossed embrace. Yet Rodin transforms literary fate into sculptural exaltation. The female nude, derived from the sensuous Torse d'Adèle — named after Adèle Abruzzesi, one of Rodin's most favoured Italian models — arches upward with luminous abandon, while the male figure responds in a sweeping counter-curve, his body seemingly suspended in air. Their union is both precarious and ecstatic, poised at the threshold between physical gravity and emotional transcendence. | | Rodin often described his working method as one of perpetual revision, likening sculpture to a language whose grammar and syntax could be endlessly reconfigured. Figures were reused, adapted and recombined in an ongoing search for expressive truth. In Eternal printemps, this process reaches an extraordinary synthesis: concave and convex forms interlock in a tightly coiled rhythm, while the lovers balance upon a rough, insufficient base that heightens the sensation of motion and risk. The male figure's feet barely touch the ground — one hovering in space, the other hanging over the edge — so that the woman's kneeling body becomes his sole anchor. | | The emotional charge of the work is inseparable from Rodin's relationship with Claudel. Their affair, which began soon after her arrival in his studio in 1882, marked one of the most fertile periods of mutual influence in modern sculpture. Claudel's own works — most notably Sakuntala (1886) and La Valse (1889) — echo the same entwined dynamism and crossed structural axes that animate Eternal printemps, suggesting a shared sculptural vocabulary developed in near tandem. In a letter written to Claudel in 1886, Rodin spoke of his "furious love" and "violent passion" — words that find palpable form in the sculpture's outstretched arms and charged interdependence. | | Rodin later claimed that the idea for Eternal printemps came to him while listening to Ludwig van Beethoven's Symphony No. 2. Reflecting on the music, he remarked on the suffering embedded within its exuberance, and on how this paradox inspired the sculptural vision he would realise. The work was also known under alternative mythological titles — Zéphyr et la Terre and Cupidon et Psyché — a strategy that allowed Rodin to cloak its overt eroticism within the legitimising framework of classical allegory. | | The sculpture's early reception cemented its significance. In 1886, Rodin presented a plaster cast of Eternal printemps to Robert Louis Stevenson, in gratitude for a public defence of his work in the London press. The group was exhibited at the Salon of 1897, and its immediate popularity prompted Rodin to authorise multiple versions. A second iteration, featuring an enlarged base and rocky support, became the model for the editions produced by the Barbedienne foundry between 1898 and 1918, following Rodin's exclusive contract with Gustave Leblanc-Barbedienne. These casts, produced in four sizes, ensured the sculpture's widespread dissemination while retaining the expressive daring of the original conception. | | At the heart of Eternal printemps lies a rare union of lyricism and tension. The lovers' embrace is not static but charged with anticipation, as though caught in the suspended instant before complete surrender. The gesture of the male figure's raised arm — curved, open, unresolved — infuses the composition with a sense of emotional propulsion that seems to lift the figures beyond the limits of the physical world. As critics have observed, Rodin here gives sculptural form to extreme states of feeling, allowing passion itself to shape space and mass. | | Eternal printemps stands as one of Rodin's most enduring images of love: ardent yet fragile, sensual yet monumental. Born from personal passion and refined through relentless formal experimentation, it distils the sculptor's belief that human emotion — when rendered with honesty and intensity — could achieve the timelessness of myth. In this work, a fleeting moment of embrace becomes eternity itself.

provenance: Otto Charles Gutekunst Collection, London (possibly acquired by 1917). | Lina Louise S. Sanders, 'Auguste Rodin', in Wasserman (ed.), Metamorphoses in Nineteenth-Century Sculpture, exh. cat., Fogg Art Museum, Cambridge, 1975, pp. 154-165 (other casts illustrated pp. 154 & 156). | J. L. Tancock, The Sculpture of Auguste Rodin, Philadelphia, 1976, no. 79-2 (another cast illustrated p. 477). | A. Le Normand-Romain, The Bronzes of Rodin, Catalogue of Works in the Musée Rodin, Vol. II, Paris, 2007, pp. 413-414 & 417-419 (another cast illustrated p. 417, fig. 4). | | | That mask determined all my future work. It is the first good piece of modelling I ever did. From that time I sought to look all around my work, to draw it well in every respect. I have kept that mask before my mind in everything I have done... In fact, I have never succeeded in making a figure as good as 'The Broken Nose'. | - Auguste Rodin | | | Conceived at the very outset of his career, Masque de l'Homme au nez cassé is widely regarded as Rodin's first true masterpiece and a work against which he measured his sculpture for decades thereafter. As an early experiment, it announces with startling clarity the artistic principles that would define Rodin's revolution of modern sculpture: truth to life, psychological depth, and a fearless rejection of academic idealisation. | | The model for the work was an ageing Parisian labourer known as Bibi, whose battered features — most notably his broken nose — bore the visible marks of a life lived hard. Rodin was drawn precisely to this physical history. Yet rather than presenting the sitter as a figure of social realism alone, he deliberately fused contemporary observation with classical allusion. The hair is arranged in a stylised manner, bound with a fillet evocative of ancient Greek portrait busts, subtly aligning this anonymous working man with the lineage of philosophers and sages from antiquity. In this physiognomic frankness — where so-called ugliness becomes a bearer of wisdom — Rodin evokes the tradition of ancient portraits of figures such as Socrates and Roman marble heads, elevating character and experience above ideal beauty. In doing so, he bridged the perceived divide between the modern streets of Paris and the timeless human condition. | | This tension lay at the heart of the work's initial rejection. When submitted to the Salon in 1864, the sculpture was refused, reportedly criticised for its unvarnished realism and fragmentary character. At a moment when French academic sculpture remained wedded to smooth ideal forms, Rodin's insistence on fractured surfaces, asymmetry and expressive modelling proved unsettling — a reaction intensified by contemporary anxieties surrounding Social Realism. The refusal was emblematic of the institutional resistance he would face repeatedly in his early career, and it would be more than a decade before he submitted another sculpture to the Salon, returning in 1875 with a marble version of L'Homme au nez cassé, which was finally accepted. | | The fragmentary nature of the mask is itself integral to its power. According to contemporary accounts, the original plaster bust partially collapsed during an exceptionally harsh winter, when Rodin was working in a poorly heated makeshift studio. Rather than discarding the damaged work, he chose to preserve and develop the mask alone. This decision — radical for the 1860s — reveals Rodin's early understanding that a fragment could convey greater intensity than a finished whole. The truncated form concentrates attention on the face, amplifying its psychological immediacy and sculptural force. In this respect, Rodin's approach resonates with his profound admiration for Michelangelo, whose unfinished Slaves, encountered in the Louvre, demonstrated how incompletion could heighten expressive power and emotional truth. | | Technically, the work demonstrates Rodin's deep engagement with historical sculptural practices. He revived the ancient method of modelling by profiles, constructing the form through successive viewpoints rather than submitting to a single frontal ideal — a practice so convincingly rediscovered that, in 1878, the sculptor Jules Desbois famously passed the work off as an antique to his fellow students at the École des Beaux-Arts. The surface remains animated and irregular, bearing the imprint of the artist's hand and resisting the polished finish prized by academic convention. Far from diminishing the sitter, this treatment imbues the mask with remarkable dignity and humanity, suggesting an implicit tenderness beneath its rugged exterior. Classical structure is thus infused with a distinctly modern vision of Paris and its eclectic cast of characters, recalling the incisive social observation found in the work of Honoré Daumier. | | Rodin himself considered L'Homme au nez cassé a foundational work, cherishing it throughout his life, carefully restoring the damaged model and returning to the subject in multiple variations. Its reputation grew steadily: the sculpture won a gold medal in Nice in 1880, was exhibited at the Grosvenor Gallery in London in 1882 — where it was admired by leading figures including Sir Frederick Leighton, who acquired a cast for himself — and appeared in progressive exhibitions such as the Salon des XX in Brussels in 1887. The work exists in numerous versions, distinguished by subtle variations in format and modelling; however, casts of the type I, premier modèle remain closest to Rodin's original conception and are especially prized for their immediacy. Closely related examples are held today in major institutional collections, including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Ashmolean Museum, and the Harvard Art Museums. | | The importance of the present cast is further underscored by its distinguished provenance. The first documented owner was Otto Charles Henry Gutekunst, the influential British art dealer, collector and co-owner of P. & D. Colnaghi & Co., whose collection included significant Old Master and modern works. While the absence of earlier provenance prevents the identification of the sculpture's initial buyer, the present work appears to be identical to the cast made by Gruet Jeune and given by Rodin in 1884 to the artists Jean-Charles Cazin and Marie Cazin. | | Masque de l'Homme au nez cassé is widely recognised as a critical turning point in nineteenth-century sculpture. It announces Rodin's break from academic orthodoxy and his emergence as an artist capable of uniting realism, classicism and psychological insight within a single form. More restrained and introspective than the expressive dynamism of later works such as L'Éternel Printemps, the mask nevertheless possesses a quiet radicalism. In its uncompromising humanity, it stands as a powerful assertion of Rodin's belief that modern sculpture must begin not with ideal beauty, but with lived experience.
