artwork_title: Working Model for Lesson of a Disaster
provenance: The artist's estate. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Exhibited | Moscow, Moscow Museum of Modern Art, Jacques Lipchitz (1891-1973), A Retrospective, 27 November 2018 – 3 March 2019. | | Literature | A.G. Wilkinson, Jacques Lipchitz, A Life in Sculpture, exh. cat., Art Gallery of Ontario, Toronto, 1989, no. 112 (another cast illustrated p. 151). | A.G. Wilkinson, The Sculpture of Jacques Lipchitz, A Catalogue Raisonné, Vol. II, The American Years, 1941-1973, New York, 2000, no. 571 (another cast illustrated p. 77). | | | On Saturday, 5 January 1952, fire tore through the studio of Jacques Lipchitz on East 23rd Street in Manhattan. Flames consumed plaster models, preparatory drawings, and works that traced decades of artistic labour, leaving behind a scene of devastation that marked one of the most traumatic moments of the sculptor's life. Among the losses were works from Lipchitz's own permanent collection — cherished pieces by Chaïm Soutine, Paul Cézanne, Juan Gris and Pablo Picasso, brought with him to New York from France. Even more devastating was the destruction of nearly ten years of work produced in New York: plaster and compositional models for sculptures already housed in major museum collections, alongside innumerable drawings that mapped the evolution of his ideas. At the age of sixty, Lipchitz found himself forced to begin again. | | The fire also claimed one of the most important commissions of his late career: the figure of the Virgin for the Church of Notre-Dame-de-Toute-Grâce at Assy, known as Notre-Dame de Liesse. Executed in plasticine and representing nearly a year of concentrated work – due to be completed within three months – the sculpture was lost. Friends and critics alike drew parallels between this loss and the Old Testament story of the Burning Bush, a comparison that resonated deeply with Lipchitz himself. Lipchitz' Virgin, consumed by fire, was imagined as purified rather than annihilated, destined to rise again transformed. The disaster also recalled an earlier trauma from Lipchitz's life: the burning of his family's hotel in his hometown of Druskininkai in 1905, an event that had already impressed upon him the fragility of material security. | | In the immediate aftermath of the 1952 fire, Lipchitz passed through a period of intense grief. Yet he came to understand the fire as a trial of faith — an ordeal that, paradoxically, illuminated the future. He resolved to remake the Virgin and his other works with renewed force and beauty, as though they might rise from the flames strengthened rather than diminished. What followed was an extraordinary outpouring of support from the American artistic community and the public at large. The Museum of Modern Art organised aid in the form of a loan, repayable through works of art — the only assistance Lipchitz was willing to accept. Lipchitz' trusted dealers, including Curt Valentin, waived their usual commissions, while others immediately commissioned new sculptures and portraits. Funds were raised toward the construction of a new studio in Hastings-on-Hudson, where Lipchitz would eventually relocate in 1953. Letters arrived from members of the public enclosing cash, cheques, and messages of goodwill. This experience of profound human kindness deeply ingratiated Lipchitz with the American public and reinforced his determination to continue. | | Central to his recovery was John Spring of the Modern Art Foundry on Long Island, who had cast the majority of Lipchitz's bronzes since his arrival in the United States. The two men shared a close friendship: Lipchitz had helped save Spring from bankruptcy in 1946, and by the early 1950s the foundry had grown into one of the most important in the country. In a gesture of solidarity, Spring gave Lipchitz a room within the foundry and allowed him to use it as a temporary studio. It was here, amid the industrial rhythms of casting and fabrication, that the ideas for Lesson of a Disaster began to take form, born directly from the imagery of the burning Virgin. The experience revealed the buoyancy of Lipchitz's nature — his capacity to rise above repeated catastrophes and emerge with renewed creative intensity. Far from diminishing his artistic powers, the disaster endowed his work with greater depth, gravity and emotional resonance. | | Conceived over the following years and developed throughout the 1960s, the Lesson of a Disaster sculptures stand as Lipchitz's deeply personal meditation on destruction and renewal. The experience of loss is transformed into a monumental allegory of regeneration. Central to the series is the figure of the phoenix, rising from a chalice-like base engulfed in flames — a symbol at once ancient and autobiographical, embodying endurance through transformation. The present work, a Working Model for Lesson of a Disaster, occupies a crucial position within this sequence, capturing the sculptor's ideas at a moment of heightened conceptual intensity and formal exploration. | | At nearly two metres in height, the sculpture commands space with an imposing verticality. Its structure recalls a medieval reliquary or ritual vessel, its lower form solid and weight-bearing, from which erupt twisting tongues of flame. From this tumult emerges the phoenix, its wings unfurling upward in an emphatic gesture of ascent. Lipchitz arrived at this form through an experimental working method that involved suspending the upper portion of the original plaster with chains — a technique he employed to explore balance, tension and gravity. From this suspended mass, the full shape gradually revealed itself to him as chalice-like in nature. | | The work draws upon a constellation of ideas: reflections on the songs and rituals of so-called primitive cultures; meditations on the regulations and taboos that had shaped the early development of Cubism; and a growing desire to move toward a more lyrical, unified sculptural language. This shift marked a release from what Lipchitz later described as the "dictatorship" of Cubism, allowing symbolic and organic forms to reassert themselves. The phoenix itself represents a synthesis of imagery — integrating the Christian dove, the Virgin as a metaphor for humanity, and a broader constellation of mythic symbols. Lipchitz did not conceive the sculpture as strictly religious, but rather as an interwoven grouping of signs: a pair of lovers embedded within the tongues of flame; the phoenix feeding a nest of small birds; fire transmuted into blossoming flower. At a later stage, he described the structure as resembling a growing plant supported on the legs of an animal — a living organism in the midst of transformation. Throughout, the imagery speaks to hope, continuity and renewal in the aftermath of catastrophe. | | The present sculpture thereby offers a particularly revealing insight into Lipchitz's sculptural thinking. It retains a sense of immediacy that reflects the artist's intense engagement with process — forms asserted, tested and reworked, symbolism held in a state of charged openness. The scale itself is striking: far from a modest maquette, this is a commanding work that bridges the intimacy of the studio and the ambition of monumental sculpture. It embodies the precise moment at which personal experience is transmuted into a universal statement. | | Lipchitz's involvement in the casting process was famously exacting. At the Modern Art Foundry and elsewhere, he acted as a major-domo, supervising every stage of production at length. He carried out repairs to models himself, hammered and filed bronze casts by hand, and applied patinas with the sensibility of a painter — selecting tones ranging from bright gold to reddish browns to complement the mood and scale of each work. There is a poetry to this process, a mastery of bronze that exploits its full expressive potential. An intensely physical modeller, Lipchitz favoured the immediacy of building and reworking forms over the slower discipline of direct carving, which he found contrary to his creative rhythm. | | The Lesson of a Disaster series belongs to Lipchitz's American years, a period marked by a profound evolution in both language and outlook. Born Chaïm Jacob Lipchitz in Lithuania to a prosperous Jewish family, his life was shaped early by a prophecy delivered by a revered rabbi, who declared that the child "should become a great person." Lipchitz later recalled how these words profoundly influenced his sense of destiny, instilling in him a belief that he was guided by something miraculous, sustained by a conviction that allowed him to persevere through repeated adversity. His early years unfolded under the shadow of anti-Semitism in the Tsarist regime, which restricted Jewish life and barred him from formal education at the St Petersburg Academy of Arts. | | Driven by ambition and resilience, Lipchitz left for Paris in 1909, immersing himself in study at the École des Beaux-Arts, the Académie Julian and the Académie Colarossi. There he absorbed the radical theories of the avant-garde: Cubism emerged as a dominant force, Italian Futurism exerted a powerful presence, and encounters with artists such as Archipenko, Boccioni, Brâncuși and Gris proved formative. From these influences, Lipchitz developed a distinctive set of enduring concerns — the human figure, classical myth, biblical themes and portraiture — providing fertile ground for the technical innovation and symbolic depth that would define his mature work. | | The importance of the Lesson of a Disaster series is underscored by its institutional recognition. Casts from the series are held in major museum collections and have been exhibited internationally in retrospectives devoted to Lipchitz's life and oeuvre. The present Working Model relates directly to these monumental statements, forming an eloquent expression of Lipchitz's late philosophy. Forged in the aftermath of catastrophe, the sculpture looks resolutely forward — a meditation on endurance, resilience and the capacity of art to transform loss into meaning. In shaping personal disaster into a universal emblem of renewal, Lipchitz created a work that carries forward both the intimacy of lived experience and the enduring power of myth.
